sections.body_md:
Standard form describes the feasible set by \(Ax = b\) and \(x \ge 0\). Assume \(A\) has full row rank, with \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns, and \(n \ge m\). A basis is a choice of \(m\) independent columns, written \(B\). The remaining columns are nonbasic.

Set the nonbasic variables to zero and solve the square system \(B x_B = b\). The solution \(x_B = B^{-1} b\), with zeros elsewhere, is a basic solution. It is a basic feasible solution when \(x_B \ge 0\). A negative entry means the columns were independent and the point is still outside the polyhedron. A zero entry among the basic variables is allowed. The point is feasible, and the basis is called degenerate.

If the feasible set is nonempty, it has at least one basic feasible solution. If in addition the linear objective is bounded below, the minimum is attained, and it is attained at a basic feasible solution. Searching the whole polyhedron can therefore be replaced by searching these points. There are finitely many bases, hence finitely many candidates, though listing all of them is not the practical algorithm.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
With the columns of \(B\) independent,
\[
x_B = B^{-1} b, \qquad x_N = 0.
\]
Feasibility is \(x_B \ge 0\). When \(B\) is diagonal with positive entries \(a\) and \(d\) and the right-hand side is \((p, q)\), the basic variables are \(p/a\) and \(q/d\). The slack basis of \(Ax + s = b\) is the identity on the slack columns, so it is feasible exactly when \(b \ge 0\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(x_1 + 2x_2 + x_3 = 21\) and \(x_1 + x_2 + x_4 = 14\), and choose columns 1 and 2. The basis matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), with determinant \(-1\). Solving gives \(x_1 = 7\) and \(x_2 = 7\), both nonnegative, and the slacks are zero.

The bench sum is 14. Check the equalities: \(7 + 14 = 21\) and \(7 + 7 = 14\). A different basis, for example the two slack columns, would give a different feasible point, \(x_3 = 21\) and \(x_4 = 14\). Both points are basic and feasible. Which one is optimal depends on a cost that this construction does not use.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Invertibility is not feasibility. The determinant test and the sign test answer different questions, and both are required. A second miss is to set the basic variables to zero and solve for the others. That reverses the definition and usually violates the equalities. A third is to treat a feasible point with more than \(m\) positive variables as basic. It can be a convex combination of basic feasible solutions, and then it is not extreme. A fourth is to reject a basic variable that equals zero. Zero is nonnegative. The basis is degenerate, and it is still feasible.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Neighboring bases differ by one column. The edge between the two basic feasible solutions is a feasible direction, and the reduced cost says whether the objective falls along that edge. The ratio test says how far the step can go before a variable hits zero. If no basis is obvious, because the right-hand side is not nonnegative in slack form, an auxiliary problem builds the first basic feasible solution or proves that none exists.
